# What Size Power Station You Need for a Fridge

**Short answer:** For a typical full-size refrigerator, get a station with **at least 1,200–1,500 W of surge**, a **pure sine wave** inverter, and **about 1,000 Wh for most of a day** or **1,400–2,000 Wh for a full 24 hours**. Each additional day needs roughly the same capacity again.

## The three checks

1. **Continuous output (W).** A modern full-size fridge draws about 100–250 W while the compressor runs. Almost any 1,000 W-class station handles that. ([BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage))
2. **Surge output (W).** This is the check that most often rules a station out. When the compressor starts, it briefly pulls several times its running watts. Estimates range from about 900–1,200 W ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)) to 1,200–2,400 W for large or older units ([BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). If the surge rating is too low, the station shuts off the moment the fridge tries to start, no matter how big its battery is. Some makers quote a surge figure that only applies to simple loads like heaters, not motors, so leave some margin.
3. **Battery capacity (Wh).** The compressor only runs about 30–40% of the time, so a typical fridge averages about 40–70 W over a day.

## Calculate your own fridge's needs

Find the **kWh/year** figure on the fridge's yellow EnergyGuide label, then:

- **Average watts** = kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760
- **Wh needed** = average watts × hours of outage ÷ 0.85 (inverter losses) × 1.2 (20% headroom)

**Example:** An 18 cu ft ENERGY STAR fridge uses 362 kWh/year. That works out to about 41 W average, or about **1,400 Wh for 24 hours**. ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator))

A large side-by-side with an ice maker can use about twice that. A warm kitchen or frequent door opening also raises usage. You can look up your model's rating in the DOE's Refrigerator Energy Rating Search Tool. ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/how-to-size-a-portable-power-station-for-a-refrigerator-and-essential-devices/))

## Options by outage length

Runtime estimates below are from HomeGridHQ's table. They assume a 150 W fridge, a 35% duty cycle, and 85% inverter efficiency. Prices are from the sources.

| Goal | Example units | Est. fridge runtime | Price seen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Most of a day | Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh), Anker SOLIX C1000 (1,056 Wh) | ~17 hrs | ~$470–$499 |
| Full day+ | Anker SOLIX F1500 (1,536 Wh, 2,400 W surge) | ~25 hrs | $599.99 at Anker ([listing](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)) |
| 1.5 days, expandable | BLUETTI AC200L (2,048 Wh, 3,600 W lifting, expands to 8 kWh) | ~33 hrs | $899 |
| Multi-day | BLUETTI Elite 300 (3,014 Wh), EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 (4,096 Wh) | 2–2.8 days | $1,199–$2,799 |

Sources: [HomeGridHQ runtime table](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) and [powerstations.reviews model list](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator).

**About the BLUETTI AC200L:** [Dealectric's page](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l) lists code **AFF5OFF** for 5% off ($899 → about $854). It says the code was tested in BLUETTI's cart on 2026-10-21. Their buy link, https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l, is an **affiliate link**, meaning they earn a commission. You can also go directly to BLUETTI's official US store and try the code there. One caveat from that page: the AC200L is rated for fewer charge cycles (3,000+) than the Elite 200 V2 (6,000+), which sells at the same price but can't be expanded.

## Tips

- **Test before an outage.** Plug the fridge into the station and confirm it starts and runs through a few compressor cycles.
- **Keep the door shut.** This greatly extends runtime.
- **Add charging if you want multi-day coverage.** Solar panels or an expansion battery are the main ways to stretch a smaller unit.

If you tell me your fridge's kWh/year (from the EnergyGuide label) and how long your outages typically last, I can narrow this down to a specific size.
